text: Bay Ganyo, having finally convinced himself that there was no possibility of settling at Jireček's as a lodger, picked up his saddlebags, without listening to the host's exhortations to leave them at his home until he found a place, and set off, accompanied by the servant, for Nàrodny Kavàrna — the café where the Bulgarian students gather. It was already seven o'clock when he entered the café with the saddlebags in hand and the kalpak on his head. Just try not to recognize who he is and where he is from! To the left of the entrance, around a table, sat several Bulgarian students.

One of them saw the entering compatriot and nudged the others: “A Bulgarian, a Bulgarian!” Everyone turned at the moment when Bay Ganyo stopped a waiter carrying a tray of coffees, and while trying as much as possible to distort the Bulgarian words to make them understandable to the foreigner, asked in a loud voice: “Deka ovde bulgarski malchiki?” — and accompanied the question with a movement of his head and his free hand. A collective laugh from the left side ended the waiter’s bewilderment. Bay Ganyo turned around and recognized his dark-eyed, dark-haired, huddled compatriots.

— Oh! Good day! So you were here? — he cried out heartily, set down the saddlebags, and began to grab the students' hands. — Why are you looking at me? Don't be afraid, I am Bulgarian... Come on, make some room for me to sit down.
— What is your name, sir? — one of the students inquired curiously.
— Me? Why do you ask? Ganyo Balkanski. I brought a little rose oil to your Prague — here it is, in the saddlebags.
— Is that so? — cried out one of the younger students in patriotic ecstasy. — Let's see it.
He really had only heard of rose oil.
— What is there to look at, it's just oil like any other — answered Bay Ganyo, — it's not for you. Leave the oil alone and tell me something else: where should I stay? I was just at Bay Irechek's...
— Is that so? — the excited student cried out again.

— What do you mean "is that so"? Why shouldn't I go to him? I went — thinking he would show some humanity, invite me to his home as a guest. Such faith! My apartment is cramped, he says, and then I don't know what, and then I don't know what else. He loved Bulgarians, he says... Him?! When there is a profit to be made, even your Uncle Ganyo knows how to love. — Is this how a Bulgarian is welcomed? A Bulgarian!... Not to lie to you, the man did feed me. And what food it was — oh well, forget it!... Bulgarians are much more hospitable; a Bulgarian, even if he has only one room, will still invite you in...

Some of the students began to realize what Bay Ganyo was driving at and were waiting from minute to minute for him to show his hand. Only the over-excited student reacted sympathetically to his words and openly shared his indignation at the inhospitality of the foreigners.
— Indeed, our Bulgarians are very hospitable — he confirmed with the greatest confidence — the locals here don't want to know you. We just hang around here in the cafes...

The student who said these words was very advanced in civilization, but for some reason did not enjoy a particular reputation among his comrades; it appeared that some sins lay upon his soul; they said, among other things, that he loved very much "to strike a bargain." It is no wonder! This wretched sin—stinginess—through the contagion of the surrounding domestic environment, takes root almost from childhood years; it withers the soul of the young man, turning him into the coldest egoist: nothing tender, nothing noble remains in him. Material interest governs all the actions of the miser and determines his relations toward those around him: no moral impulse precedes, no remorse follows his actions, which are directed without discrimination of means toward obtaining benefits. Even then, when these actions bring disaster or disgrace upon someone, even then, instead of remorse, the egoist-miser feels satisfaction, as if the loss of others is his gain, the misfortune of others is his happiness. One thing would disturb our young egoist—to be outwitted by someone. While among other nations the word "cunning" is synonymous with devious or treacherous, and when attached to a person, would lower them in the opinion of society, among us people adorn themselves with the epithet "cunning" as if with the most honorable decoration: "Look at that! A cunning boy he turned out to be, long life to his father, he deceived us all! We couldn't trick him! Well done. Bravo!"

No actions or relationships made sense to Bodkov—that was his name—if they did not result in some windfall, some easy profit. (Are there words in European languages corresponding to these, in this meaning of theirs?) If he visited the families there, he did not do so out of sociability, out of a desire to become acquainted with the way of life in more civilized circles; the intellectual and moral interests of that society not only failed to occupy him but were a burden to him—they were like boring intervals, unbearable pauses that separated him from the goal of his visits—from the windfall: be it some little feast or some outing at their expense. He could not imagine an acquaintance with women without ulterior motives. He kept a whole list of maidens—which one had how much dowry; nothing else interested him in this regard. Likewise, self-interest determined his relations with his comrades. Flattery, slander, petty intrigues, and denunciations were the tools of his gains. Even such things as national and tribal sympathies and antipathies served him only to extract personal benefit. More than once he had dipped into the purses of various Slavic committees, now as "from Batak," now as an "emigrant." But at these matters, Aslanov is more of a master.

Such was the exalted student who supported Bay Ganyo in his opinion of the hospitality of foreigners. — Yes, we hang around here in the cafes, no one invites us over — he repeated to please Bay Ganyo.

— "And where do you want them to leave you to rot?" spoke up with a contemptuous smile a student with a bilious look, who, it seemed, had long harbored a hatred for the young egoist. — "Do you want them to carry you on their hands? Why? Is it because, before you’ve even crossed the threshold of their house, you’ll first hit on the maid who meets you in the hallway? Is it because in their company you either stand silent as an oak, or open your mouth only to babble vulgarities and nonsense? Is it because you’ll praise them to the heavens to their faces, only to slander them behind their backs? Is it because you’ll throw dust in their eyes and present yourself as the son of a millionaire manufacturer or a shipowner, when your father only has two braid-spinning wheels or two leaky vats—just so you can charm the parents and seduce their daughter? Why should they receive you with open arms? Who are you? What are you to them? Whose face are you shoving your hospitality into? And what is this over-praised hospitality of yours! — Is it that the Bulgarian will lay out a greasy bed for you and cover you with a questionable rag? Ah, for God’s sake, stop these savage boastings! Isn’t it time we finally opened our eyes?"
— Why are you so fired up? Is now the time you found to argue — one of the students spoke up — when we have a guest?

— Let the man talk a bit, he’s not asking for money, is he? — Bay Ganyo reassured him with this typical argument: “H e  i s n’ t  a s k i n g  f o r  m o n e y,  i s  h e!” He can say whatever he wants, do whatever he wants, as long as he doesn't ask for money, as long as he doesn't touch our pocket, our interests. He might even lie, he’s not asking for money, is he!

But after this accidental incident, a friendly conversation could no longer be maintained. The group grew quiet, and one by one, they began to disperse. Of the Bulgarians, only Bai Ganyo and the overexcited student remained, the latter not wanting to miss the opportunity to derive some benefit from his chance encounter with the Bulgarian rose oil merchant. — The pot rolled along and found its lid.

Not an hour had passed, and the student managed to slander his comrades before Bay Ganyo so much that he made him cry out from the bottom of his heart: "Well done, you rascals!" After another hour, Bay Ganyo was already in the student's room, who knew how to quite skillfully exploit the arrival of the guest to his own advantage, recommending him to his landlords as his relative, a millionaire who "owns a bunch of rose oil factories." He managed to borrow ten guilders from the landlady—to whom he hadn't paid the room rent for quite a long time. While in one room the student was extolling Bay Ganyo's riches, in the neighboring room Bay Ganyo had already taken off his *anteriya* and was searching for something in it with great attention, muttering under his breath: "Those damn vermin have bred again." The concept of cleanliness is not developed to a very high degree in Bay Ganyo. "Can a living person ever be without vermin?"—say the old folk in our parts, and calmed by this axiom, they do not hinder the reproduction of the little creatures too zealously. And why should they deprive themselves of such a pleasure: the sun has come out, and what is that sun for if he cannot go out onto the veranda, stretch out on the mat, sneeze two or three times from its dust, and have his grandmother come, and lay his head on her knee, and she sticks her bony fingers with mourning nails into his hair and, as if sorting rice, begins—click!—here, click!—there, and when the little creatures get scared and crawl over his head, what a pleasant tickling, and then the grandmother starts to sing, and that Balkan sun of yours is shining! An idyll...

Bay Ganyo, after finishing his entomological investigations, restored his attire and, without knocking, entered the adjacent room, but immediately cried out: "Pardon!" — and with good reason: he found the student and the landlady's daughter in a very tender vis-à-vis — they were embracing, as befits two young hearts in love. The girl, ashamed, fled into the other room.
— Hey, why do you come in like that? You embarrassed the girl — said the student with an ironic wink.
— You've hit the jackpot! — Bai Ganyo whispered mysteriously, his eyes shining like those of a monastery tomcat. — A sleek one, devil take her! Is she a servant?
— What a servant! The landlady's daughter!

— Is that so? Here you can't tell them apart, which one is a servant, which one is a mistress; all polished, all cleanly dressed. One comes across you, grinning so smarmily, you think she’s a servant, you tease her, and you bring trouble on your head; another one comes along, pretty, humble, you think, ha, this is the mistress, you stand up for her, invite her to sit, she’s shy—naturally!—you talk to her with etiquette, and then later you see her cleaning your boots!

From the student’s stories, accompanied by various gestures with which he embellished and gave more force and meaning to his words, Bay Ganyo learned that for several months the young man, under the guise of pure love, had been attacking with irresistible persistence the daughter of his widowed landlady.

— And she, the fool," the narrator explains, "hopes that I will take her as my wife! Let her hope, and let her feed me well, let her sew shirts for me. If she were some rich woman—I could understand a man taking her, but she’s a pauper like me. She fawns over me because she thinks I’m a rich man. If she only knew what I really am, would she be so eager? The local women here are terrible schemers! But I know how to play them, don't I?" — And he went on to explain at length and in detail how he plays them...
— Bravo! — cried Bay Ganyo with oily eyes, delighted by the young interlocutor.

— Wait a minute, is that all? If that's all, it's nothing! There's another one, another one I've got my eye on, but who knows! If I could only turn her head—there's a real prize to be had there. Rich! I'm invited to their place tomorrow; they're taking me for a trip to a village.
— "And when are you going to take me to the factories?" asked the practical Bay Ganyo.

— Easy enough, the day after tomorrow. You stay here tomorrow, hang around them; when they see that you don't know the language, they won't let you go to the inn, they'll invite you to their place and you'll eat for free.

And indeed, early the next morning, the student went out to visit, while Bai Ganyo remained in the lodging alone with the hosts. As usual, on this day too, he rose very early, woke and saw off his companion, and waited for another whole hour until the landladies woke up. This waiting was very difficult for him; he felt a great need, like any human being, but he had forgotten to ask the student where *that* was and—willy-nilly—he had to wait for the household to get up and—shame or no shame—ask them. It is very bad when a person does not know the language abroad; for the simplest thing, they cannot understand you, you always have to explain with your hands, with your fingers, to show them... And yet, can everything be shown? Bai Ganyo knew languages; he could talk to you in Turkish like a Turk, he understood Vlach, Serbian, Russian every now and then, but the Germans and the Czechs do not understand a single one of these languages. It could not be said that Bai Ganyo did not know German at all; he knew a word or two.

In the neighboring room, the hostesses got up and began to stir. Bay Ganyo looked through the keyhole, not out of any improper curiosity, but to see if they were already dressed, and carefully, with bated breath, as he familiarized himself with their toilet, he was composing in his mind a phrase in German that would correspond to our: “Where is that thing, for the big business?” — and finally, from the literal translation, he combined the phrase: “Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit?” — Knock! knock! knock!
— Come in! — two female voices called out from the next room.
Bay Ganyo opened the door, said a “pardon” and shyly uttered: — Wo is diese fur gross Arbeit? — and wiggled his fingers to emphasize the question.
— Co, pan? — the girl asked in bewilderment, as she tried to examine the appearance of the millionaire recommended by her lover.
— Fur gross Arbeit? — repeated Bay Ganyo, even more embarrassed, and again gestured with his fingers and his head, but noticed that they did not understand him.
They understood him, but not as they should have; the women thought that he was informing them that he had come to do great things, a large trade in rose oil.

"Damn it! — Bay Ganyo thinks to himself. — What should I do now?" — And so that at least the daughter would not be a witness to his predicament, he beckoned the mother into his room, closed the door, and after repeating the question in German once more, supplemented it this time with a desperate gesture that made the lady flee to the other room, choking with suppressed laughter. The maid appeared and satisfied Bay Ganyo's curiosity. A trio of continuous female laughter shook the walls.
The aroma coming through the open kitchen doors into the corridor whetted Bay Ganyo's appetite, and out of curiosity, he peeked in to see what they were cooking. The hostess and the maid were there.

— Was ist das? — asked Bay Ganyo in a condescending tone, not so much out of a desire to acquaint himself with the culinary art of the Czechs, as to show that he had been around Europe and knew his way around these things, and that he also knew how to speak German. — Soup, right? You're cooking soup? I know. Ich versten supa!

And Bay Ganyo, with a mixture of German, Bulgarian, and distorted Bulgarian, aided by impressive gestures, let the landlady understand that he would not refuse to try the taste of their cuisine. Seeing that the women showed a greater inclination to explain themselves in Czech, Bay Ganyo also turned to "Czech" and supported his condescending desire with the words: "ya hochem kushay," interpreting these words by repeatedly touching his fingers to his open mouth, and then, pointing to his three fingers, he poked his chest with his index finger, poked the same finger toward the landlady's chest, and a third time pointed into space, as if pointing to the landlady's invisible daughter, i.e., "to eat together, the three of us!" For Bay Ganyo, it was also important to know at what hour he would have lunch, as he intended to go for a walk, so as not to miss the meal, and then "pay for food, while there is free stuff, a windfall," and therefore he took out his huge watch and, holding it under the landlady's nose, made her show him with her finger on the hands when he would "kushay." When he was convinced that everything was in order, Bay Ganyo went into his room, stuffed the vials into his sash, and went out into the street for a walk, so that he could both take a stroll and perhaps stumble upon a customer for rose oil.

Bai Ganyo sees that many streets intersect, one could take the wrong path, one could get lost, and as a practical man he looked around to notice some sign by which he could recognize the house, and saw on the opposite side, on a back wall, an inscription in large letters; he took out his notebook, licked his pencil, wrote an exact copy of the inscription and, fully confident that he had in his hands the most accurate address of his lodgings, set off through the narrow streets of old Prague, now looking at this, now looking at that, a customer here, a customer there—he got carried away, and not only did he get carried away, but he lost his way. What now? And as he started looking for his house, and as he got even more bogged down in the Jewish streets, an hour passed, two hours passed, he hit a dead-end at some house—no exit, he went in another direction, walked and walked and popped out on the banks of the Vltava. “Oh, the devil, what now?” And never mind that, but lunchtime came, came and went. Our Bai Ganyo had tucked up his clothes, he strode and strode, became soaking wet, out of breath, looking like a sight. The people he met, especially the policemen, looked at him suspiciously: this troubled him even more. “Oh, the devil, what now?” And he was hungry, a revolution in his stomach, but why the devil would he throw his money to the wind when he was invited to lunch?

But, you will say, why is Bay Ganyo wandering the streets when the address is in his pocket? Well, that's just the thing! And Bay Ganyo is no fool; do you really think he didn't think to take out his notebook, stop this person or that on the street, and by pointing to the written address, ask them with his fingers "which way"? He knows these things; he stops both men and women, but a strange thing — whomever he stops to ask, as soon as he points to what is written, they either look at him in wonder and laugh, or turn away from him with indignation. One lady, probably some nervous old maid, when he showed her the address, snapped at him so sharply that even Bay Ganyo lost his courage. "The devil take it, either I'm crazy, or all of Prague has gone mad," he thinks to himself, unable to cease wondering at the effect his written address produces; while thinking, he looks around and suddenly — isn't this luck? — he sees, looming before him, the Národní Kavárna, the café where the Bulgarian students gather. Bay Ganyo goes inside and finds the angry student.
— Good day! Tell me, your honor, am I crazy, or are the people here crazy? — asks Bay Ganyo, out of breath, with wet hair clinging to his forehead.
The student looked at him questioningly. Bay Ganyo told him how he had gotten lost, how he had inquired about his house by the address, and what they had replied to him.
The student, knowing that the Czechs, rude and fanatical only toward the Germans, are otherwise quite polite, cannot help but wonder how they could fail to be of service to Bay Ganyo.
— Read what's written here, please! — and Bay Ganyo held out the notebook.
The student read it: at first he frowned a bit, then he burst out laughing!...
— Did you show this address to some lady? — he asked through his laughter.
— Why? I showed it, didn't I! Well?
— Well? Do you know what is written here?
— What?
— It is written "...Zde je zapovedeno..." "Here it is forbidden to..." You copied it from some wall.
— You don't say! Look! Tsk... tsk... tsk! Are you telling the truth? Look! — said Bai Ganyo, clicked his tongue a little, and then he too began to laugh.

The student did not know Bodkov’s lodgings—they did not visit one another—and so he advised Bay Ganyo to wait, as some Bulgarian or other was bound to come along and show him the house. It is easy to say “wait,” but let us see if Bay Ganyo’s stomach was of the same opinion! And that it was not of the same opinion, it proved demonstratively with an incessant rumbling.
"— Are you hungry? — the student asked him, hearing the revolutionary signals."

— Who, me? — I'm not — Bay Ganyo lied a little, because if he told the truth, the other would show him the inn, and it wouldn't do at all to admit to him (“How can I tell such a stubborn kid!”) that a free meal awaited him at the landladies' place.

A conversation between Bay Ganyo and the "stubborn kid" could not be struck up. From the first meeting and somehow instinctively, they sensed that they were not for each other, because according to the Bulgarian proverb (oh, what exquisite proverbs the Bulgarian genius has created!) "scabby donkeys can smell each other across nine hills." One had come from Bulgaria, the other had lived in Europe; surely there would have been something to talk about, since there must be some small difference between the West and our fatherland. However, Bay Ganyo did not sense this difference, and how could he! Wherever he goes, he carries with him his own atmosphere, his own manners and customs; he seeks lodging according to his own tastes, meets only his own kind of people to whom he is accustomed and in whom, of course, he sees nothing new: if he goes to Vienna, he will stay at the "London" hotel; it is just as stuffy there, smells just as much of the kitchen and hydrogen sulfide as it does at home; he meets the same Turks, Armenians, Serbs, and Albanians he is used to meeting every day; he will not go to the "Habsburg" café because he is afraid they will fleece him, but will enter the Greek café again, which is just as unclean and stifled by eternal smoke as our own cafés are. If he goes for trade, he will go to the Bulgarian merchants, and through them, he does not even realize that he is coming into contact with Europeans. And that it is precisely outside this limited sphere that European life begins, he neither knows nor, it seems, even wants to know. The upbringing, the moral world of the European, his domestic environment—the fruit of centuries-old tradition and gradual refinement—the intellectual movement, social struggles and the way they are conducted, museums, libraries, philanthropic institutions, the fine arts, and the thousands of manifestations of progress do not burden the attention of Bay Ganyo.

"As if my father was always listening to operas" — says Bay Ganyo, and charmed by this principle of fossilization and ultra-retrogradeness, he is not too startled by the "new fashion," i.e., by civilization. But despite all this, Bay Ganyo lacks the valor of the Chinese — to wall himself off with a wall against the invasion of civilization — and despite being inspired by the principle "my father didn't do this and I won't do it either," yet you suddenly see that he has put on a clean shirt, put on gloves, and when they pressure him, he even puts on a frock coat; he gets angry, he laughs, but he puts on the frock coat. You hear him saying "pardon," talking about the "constentution," boasting here and there that he loves "soup," when in fact he would prefer a spicy chorba over all European dishes.
— Ah, here comes a Bulgarian boy, he knows Bodkov's lodgings — stated the "stubborn kid"...

— "Come on, take me home," Bay Ganyo turned to the young Bulgarian in such a tone that should have disappeared even in our relations with lazy servants; but the words "politeness," "courtesy" are newly stolen from the Russian language, "delicacy" is borrowed from the French, and among us, the most suitable term for these concepts is the word "slobbering." Those soft, gentle, heartfelt forms of address, which characterize the relations of civilized people and which make life milder, more pleasant—are incomprehensible to Bay Ganyo; he speaks as God gave him: "Come on, hey, listen here, take me home." And what does it mean: "I beg of you, have the kindness, be so kind," what is all this slobbering!...

The young Bulgarian led Bay Ganyo to the gate of his lodgings and returned. Bay Ganyo looked at the wretched inscription on the opposite wall, shook his head at it threateningly, clicked his tongue, and entered the house. In the corridor he met no one; he peeked into the kitchen—there the fire was already extinguished, the dishes cleaned and arranged. "Phew, what a pity, I missed the freebie," Bay Ganyo muttered, entered his room, crouched over his saddlebags, took the vials out of his sash, stuffed them inside, pulled out the greasy kashkaval cheese, cut himself some dry bread, and began to stifle the revolution, smacking his lips so appetizingly that even the laziest Swiss cow would have envied him. To stimulate his lymphatic organs, tired from unproductive labor, he let a chewed-up Arnaut pepper pass down his esophagus, which made his eyes water and caused him to accompany his lip-smacking with a sniffle. The maid, who was tidying up in the adjacent room, hearing the strange sounds with which Bay Ganyo accompanied his snack, opened the door and peeked into the room: Bay Ganyo shyly covered the saddlebags with his back, turned his tearful and sweaty face, said: "Pardon!", sniffed energetically with his nose, and drove the maid away—that is, not that he told her to leave, but she hurried to flee, thinking that the millionaire might have received some sorrowful news.

Bodkov did not return that evening. Towards evening the hostesses came home; in the kitchen, the fire was lit again and they began to cook dinner. Bay Ganyo already considers himself one of the family, "after all, why stand on ceremony with women" — he says, and without any preamble enters the kitchen and explains more with gestures than with words that he got lost in the streets and missed lunch, but no matter — he is owed a lunch, he will make up for it with a dinner. Bay Ganyo also understands culinary art, and not only does he understand it, but any violation of this craft outrages him. He saw, for example, that the hostess was preparing to put a fresh fish into boiling water, and he rebelled with all his energy, grabbed the hostess's hand, pulled out the fish with his other hand, and made a sign with his hand and head, by which he meant to say: "Stop, don't move, just watch how fish is cooked!" "Salt!" — Bay Ganyo commands. They give him salt; he rolls up his sleeves to the elbows of his hairy arms, reaches into the salt cellar with his not-so-delicate fingers, and begins to salt and rub the already salted fish inside and out. "Red pepper!" — but where would these fools have red pepper! "Black pepper" — Bay Ganyo commands, grabs the pepper and rubs it on the fish. "Grill!" — trumpets the triumphant cook, but here they could not understand him, despite all his gestures, and he himself looked around and could not spot a grill; but is this an obstacle for Bay Ganyo? He wasn't born yesterday! Taking the tongs, he raked all the fire in front of the oven opening, left the other dishes to rest (it was a good thing they were already ready), spread the tongs, placed the fish on them, and tried to shove it into the oven, but the door was narrow, the fish got caught, slipped and — splat! — into the fire. "Oh!" — the hostess cried out. "Nothing, nothing!" — Bay Ganyo reassured her, grabbed the fish, blew off the stuck coals and ash, and put it back on the grill. Smoke and the smell of fish filled the entire kitchen. The hostesses — in despair; Bay Ganyo beams, he is now in his element; while roasting the fish, he blows and sniffs, irritated by the appetizing smoke, and at the same time commands with his free hand, greasy from turning the fish, to set the table so his dish doesn't get cold: "If fresh fish isn't hot — throw it away!" The fish, roasted, with its tail and head rolled in ash, was placed on a plate, and under Bay Ganyo's polite command: "Quick! Quick! While it's hot, give me lemon and wine; without wine, it's not worth a penny!" — they sat around the table, having sent the servant running for lemon and wine. What could they do! The millionaire wasn't going to change his habits for their pleasure, was he! The hostess reached out to cut the fish. "Please, please, please! God forbid!" — Bay Ganyo shouted and grabbed her hand, then turned the fish on its back, pressed it here and there with two fingers, and it split into two halves. Well, go ahead and try not to triumph! The servant brought a lemon; Bay Ganyo cut it, grabbed a half with his whole palm, and squeezed it over the plate with such diligence that even the pulpy parts of the lemon fell onto the fish. How do you think, does Bay Ganyo have an appetite? Hardly as much lemon juice flowed into the plate as the saliva Bay Ganyo swallowed. And wine was brought. Dinner began.

Carlsbad and I know not what other "-bad" the Aesculapians recommend to those suffering from stomach catarrh. Let them take these sufferers by the ear and seat them at the table before Bay Ganyo, and even if their stomachs are more ruined than the streets of Yuchbunar... you shall see what an effect the spectacle will have on them!... Bay Ganyo eats, man, he’s not joking; he eats so that his ears flap! All the organs of his body are in motion, with his teeth, tongue, and nose in the lead. This is where one realizes the paleness and poverty of language! With what words, what interjections, what punctuation marks, and finally, what musical notes is it possible to depict those smackings, gruntings, snifflings, clatterings, clickings, and suckings, which pour from Bay Ganyo like hail!... Lucky hostesses! Not every Czech woman will have the good fortune to enjoy such a spectacle.

They finally finished eating. They moved into the reception room. Bay Ganyo, red as a peony, kept twirling his mustache, burping into his hand, and muttering "pardon." They settled into the chairs. Bay Ganyo rolled a cigarette, greasy from his fingers, and began to puff and blow clouds of smoke through his mustache. Is this not the most opportune moment for enjoyment: for music, for songs, for love? The young lady caught the millionaire's mood and asked him if he liked music. Who? Bay Ganyo? Why, if Bay Ganyo doesn't love music, who else will? Who else has been able to instill such respect for himself in the Gypsies—that is, the musicians—as Bay Ganyo? Just let him wink an eye at them, and look what happens to those Gypsies! Fire! Fire! That violin starts to wail, that clarinet starts to shriek!
Your body is a poplar,
on my heart like two stakes.
The stitch on your dress
Burn my heart...

— Shut up, you Gypsy! I don't want love songs! Play me something for rakia! — Bay Ganyo shouted at them and banged his glass on the table. They start "The Dark Carnation," Bay Ganyo bangs his glass, they stop. They start "We want no wealth" — he bangs his glass again. They turn to "Green Leaf." "Ha, did you see that now! E-e-e-e-h! Come, my joy, come!"... — and smash the bottle on the ground or into the window... Well, who is the master of these things? And was it once, was it twice? But how would t h e s e w o m e n know who your Bay Ganyo is! And even if you tell them how many windows you've smashed to music, they can't understand you!...

— I love music! — Bay Ganyo uttered condescendingly. — I love music! — he repeated and shook his head, which in his opinion expressed the sad necessity of listening, for the sake of the women, to a miserable tinkling of a piano. “What do you understand of playing, of *mohabet*?” — thought Bay Ganyo to himself.
— "The gentleman is playing 'Bacon', mommy!" — the girl announced her discovery.
— "Bacon, indeed," Bay Ganyo spoke up, "how do you know it?"

Delighted by his success, Bay Ganyo sat on the chair to play, now with good reason, something more serious. And what could be more serious than "The Night is Terrible"? Bay Ganyo began to p l a y, but remained dissatisfied with his own performance. And quite naturally so! "The Night is Terrible" was not created for the piano; the sounds are cut short: you strike the key on "terri-i-i-ble!" and the voice breaks off; the harmonica is a different story! When you put your finger on "... ri-i-i-ble..." — press it, damn it all! Let it drone for half an hour, press it, let it roll in waves until your heart's content! But with a piano — clink, clank, nothing but wind! Bay Ganyo saw that the effect produced by "The Little Bacon" would fade; he thought and thought, then decided: "Wait, let me sing 'The Night is Terrible' to these womenfolk!..." He reflected for a moment, wanting to get into a mournful mood in the spirit of the sorrowful song, sighed deeply once, put his right hand to his ear, half-closed his eyes, and then, how he opened his maw!...

“Grandissimo maestro Verdi! You have no enemies, you cannot have enemies! But if, beyond all expectations, some monster should appear, he would be Satan himself. God is great, Esimio Maestro! — and all the arrows of the evil spirit are powerless against you! Only one... only one means can the Deceiver use, and the entire musical world will be covered in mourning... We shall pray, and you pray too, Divin Maestro, to the Almighty Creator, that He may not allow Satan to lead you into the salon where Bay Ganyo is singing ‘The night is terrible’... And when your most refined hearing is shattered by the wild, inhuman sounds incomprehensible to you, may the Evil Spirit reveal the terrible truth to you with his satanic laughter: Ha! ha! ha! Verdi! This is a song from your   d i v i n e   ‘Traviata’! Ha! ha! ha! ha-a!!...”
— It's late already, gentlemen — said the shy Ilcho, looking at his watch, — midnight! Let's go, and another time, God willing, we'll talk about Bai Ganyo again.

— Hey, Ilcho, tell me, why do you hate Bulgarian songs so much? — Dravichkata spoke up on the way out.
— Who? Me, hate them? I am sorry, my little dove, that you have misunderstood me. I am capable of admiring, of losing myself, of being enthralled to the point of ecstasy by our beautiful melancholy folk songs—but by the Bulgarian songs, and not by those loathsome parodies of foreign vulgar songs, which our Bay Ganyos present to us, twisted beyond recognition through those Gypsy appoggiaturas and throat-straining drunken trills and fiorituras... We have songs, but we have no singers. I am ready to embrace my enemy if he sings to me, as it should be sung, the song "Bogdan, May God Strike You Down" or "Roll Up Your White Sleeves, Girl Velo," and to look askance at my friend when I see him admiring "Green Leaf," "The Little Carnation," and other such Gypsy charms...
